theory.intro: If a quantity $Q$ changes at a rate proportional to how much is present, then $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$. The number $k$ is the **constant of proportionality**. This equation has solution $Q=Ae^{kt}$, where $A$ is the value of $Q$ at $t=0$.
facts: For $Q>0$, if $k>0$ the quantity grows, and if $k<0$ the quantity decays. For $Q<0$, these directions of change are reversed. If $k=0$, the quantity is constant; if $A=0$, then $Q=0$ for all $t$.
The rate is proportional to the **amount**, not to the time, so $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kt$ is a different model.
$Q=Ae^{kt}+B$ satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$ exactly when $kB=0$. When $k\ne0$, this requires $B=0$.
For $A>0$ and $k<0$ the graph falls towards the asymptote $Q=0$ but never reaches it.
One matching pair of values with $Q\ne0$ gives $k$ directly, since $k=\dfrac{1}{Q}\times\dfrac{dQ}{dt}$. When $Q=0$, the equation requires $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=0$; this pair cannot determine $k$.
If $A<0$ the whole graph lies below the $t$-axis, a reflection of the $A>0$ case.
steps: Differentiate the given function to find $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}$.
Rewrite the derivative in terms of $Q$.
State the value of $k$ and, for $Q>0$, whether the model is growth, decay or constant. For $Q<0$, use the sign of $kQ$ to describe the direction of change.

workedExamples.question_text: A quantity is modelled by $Q=18e^{-0.4t}$. Verify that it satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-0.4Q$, and state its initial value.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}\dfrac{dQ}{dt}&=-0.4\times18e^{-0.4t}\\&=-0.4Q\end{align*}$

The model satisfies the differential equation.

$\begin{align*}Q(0)&=18e^0\\&=18\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A radioactive sample initially has mass $120$ grams. Its mass decreases at a rate proportional to the mass present, with decay constant of magnitude $0.07$ per day. Write a differential equation and a formula for its mass $M$ after $t$ days.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The mass decreases, so $k=-0.07$ per day.

$\dfrac{dM}{dt}=-0.07M$

Using $M=Ae^{kt}$, the initial mass gives $A=120$.

$M=120e^{-0.07t}$ grams, for $t\ge0$.

workedExamples.question_text: The mass $M$ of a sample satisfies $\dfrac{dM}{dt}=kM$, where $t$ is measured in minutes. When its mass is $320$ grams, it is decreasing at $24$ grams per minute. Find $k$ and the rate of change when its mass is $100$ grams.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The signed rate is $-24$ grams per minute.

$\begin{align*}-24&=320k\\k&=-\dfrac{24}{320}\\&=-0.075\end{align*}$

Thus $k=-0.075$ per minute.

When $M=100$ grams:

$\begin{align*}\dfrac{dM}{dt}&=-0.075\times100\\&=-7.5\text{ g/min}\end{align*}$

The mass is decreasing at $7.5$ grams per minute.

workedExamples.question_text: Two positive quantities have models $G=30e^{0.2t}$ and $D=30e^{-0.2t}$ for $t\ge0$. Sketch both on the same axes. Explain why the growth curve becomes steeper while the decay curve becomes less steep, and identify the decay curve's horizontal asymptote.
For $k\ne0$, determine when $Q=Ae^{kt}+B$ satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$. Hence explain why $Q=14e^{0.3t}+5$ does not satisfy an equation of the form $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=cQ$ for any constant $c$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}\dfrac{dQ}{dt}&=kAe^{kt}\\&=k(Q-B)\\&=kQ-kB\end{align*}$

This equals $kQ$ exactly when $kB=0$. Since $k\ne0$, it requires $B=0$.

For $Q=14e^{0.3t}+5$:

$\begin{align*}\dfrac{dQ}{dt}&=4.2e^{0.3t}\\&=0.3(Q-5)\\&=0.3Q-1.5\end{align*}$

If this were $cQ$, then $(0.3-c)Q=1.5$ for all $t$. The quantity $Q$ varies with $t$, so no constant $c$ can satisfy this identity.

workedExamples.question_text: A quantity has model $Q=-80e^{0.15t}$ for $t\ge0$. Find its initial value and proportionality constant. Explain whether $Q$ increases or decreases as time passes.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}Q(0)&=-80e^0\\&=-80\end{align*}$

$\begin{align*}\dfrac{dQ}{dt}&=-12e^{0.15t}\\&=0.15Q\end{align*}$

Thus $A=-80$ and $k=0.15$. Since $Q<0$, the rate $0.15Q$ is negative. The quantity decreases, becoming more negative and moving farther from zero.

foundation.question_text:
A positive quantity satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-0.4Q$.
Is this growth or decay, and why?
foundation.solution_text:
$k=-0.4$
$k<0$, so the rate is negative whenever $Q$ is positive.
This is exponential decay.

foundation.question_text:
The number $N$ of bacteria increases at a rate proportional to the number present, with constant of proportionality $0.6$ per hour.
Write a differential equation for $N$.
foundation.solution_text:
The rate is proportional to the amount $N$.
$\dfrac{dN}{dt}=0.6N$

foundation.question_text:
A sample satisfies $Q=250e^{-0.15t}$ grams after $t$ hours.
State the initial mass and the value of $k$.
Show that $Q=Ae^{kt}$ satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$ for any constants $A$ and $k$.

The mass $M$ of a radioactive sample decreases at a rate proportional to the mass present, with magnitude of the decay constant $0.03$ per year.
Write a differential equation for $M$.
foundation.solution_text:
The mass is decreasing, so the constant is negative.
$\dfrac{dM}{dt}=-0.03M$

foundation.question_text:
A quantity satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=0.25Q$ and $Q=40$ when $t=0$.
Write $Q$ in terms of $t$.

development.question_text: Show that $Q=5e^{-2t}+3$ does not satisfy $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$ for any constant $k$.
development.solution_text:
$Q=5e^{-2t}+3$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-10e^{-2t}$
$5e^{-2t}=Q-3$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-2\left(Q-3\right)$
$=-2Q+6$
This is not a constant multiple of $Q$, so no value of $k$ works.

development.question_text:
A positive quantity satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=0.05Q$.
Describe the graph of $Q$ against $t$ for $t\ge 0$.
development.solution_text:
$k=0.05>0$, so $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}>0$ whenever $Q>0$.
The graph is increasing for all $t\ge 0$.
It starts at $Q=A$ when $t=0$ and rises ever more steeply, since the rate grows with $Q$.

development.question_text:
A population satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.08P$, where $P$ is measured in individuals and $t$ in years.
Find the rate of change of the population at the moment when $P=15\,000$.

A quantity is given by $Q=1800e^{-0.25t}$ litres after $t$ hours.
Find the rate of change of $Q$ at the moment when $Q=600$ litres.
development.solution_text:
$Q=1800e^{-0.25t}$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-0.25\times 1800e^{-0.25t}$
$=-0.25Q$
$\text{When }Q=600:$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-0.25\times 600$
$=-150\text{ L/h}$
The quantity is decreasing at $150$ litres per hour.

development.question_text: Verify that $Q=12e^{0.2t}$ satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=0.2Q$, and state the initial value of $Q$.

development.solution_text:
Curve $A$ has $k>0$.
For $k>0$ and $Q>0$ the rate $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$ is positive, so the curve rises.
Curve $B$ falls towards the asymptote $Q=0$, so it has $k=-0.3$.

development.question_text:
A quantity satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$.
When $Q=250$ grams, the quantity is decreasing at $20$ grams per minute.
Find $k$.

mastery.question_text: For $k\ne0$, show that $Q=Ae^{kt}+B$ satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$ only when $B=0$.
mastery.solution_text:
$Q=Ae^{kt}+B$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kAe^{kt}$
$Ae^{kt}=Q-B$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=k\left(Q-B\right)$
$=kQ-kB$
This equals $kQ$ for all $t$ only if $kB=0$, so $B=0$ when $k\ne 0$.

mastery.question_text:
A positive quantity satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-0.3Q$.
Explain why the quantity decreases more slowly as time passes.
mastery.solution_text:
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-0.3Q$, so the size of the rate is $0.3Q$.
Since $k<0$ and $Q>0$, the quantity decreases, so $Q$ gets smaller as $t$ increases.
A smaller $Q$ gives a smaller value of $0.3Q$, so the rate of decrease shrinks with the quantity.
When $Q$ halves, the rate of decrease also halves.

mastery.question_text:
A quantity is given by $Q=-50e^{0.4t}$.
Find $k$, and describe what happens to $Q$ as $t$ increases.
mastery.solution_text:
$Q=-50e^{0.4t}$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-20e^{0.4t}$
$=0.4\left(-50e^{0.4t}\right)$
$=0.4Q$
$k=0.4$
Since $A=-50<0$, $Q$ is negative for all $t$.
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}$ is negative, so $Q$ becomes more negative as $t$ increases, moving away from the asymptote $Q=0$.
